source_span: the composite PMI unexpectedly hit a 5-year high of 58.4 in September (vs. 55.3 expected). So that played into the narrative of resilient growth, which in turn would enable the Fed to keep hiking rates to deal with inflation.
source_chain: DB (17530): PMI beat (58.4 vs 55.3, 5yr high) plus an oil rebound therefore hawkish repricing of the Fed path (Oct-hike odds to 69%, year-end pricing at 37bp, near-even odds of two more hikes) therefore the biggest 10yr yield jump since April 2025 to a post-2007 high of 5.11%, worsened by a weak 5yr auction (+3.1bp tail) therefore equities sold off despite strong growth data because the level breaks valuation assumptions. Complemented by JPM (17562/17539): the same PMI beat plus the fastest input-cost inflation rise since 2020 confirm the Fed was underpricing terminal rates, and the 5yr auction's 3.20bp tail on weak end-user demand shows yields haven't found a floor, therefore JPM's house view says yields are moving toward a 5.5% fair value where, historically, such overshoots become equity buying opportunities -- but JPM stays tactically cautious until that level (or de-escalation) arrives. Invalidation: yields reaching the 5.5% fair-value anchor, or oil/geopolitical de-escalation.
pulse_chain: PMI beat (58.4 vs 55.3, DB) therefore yields to 5.11%/5.16% (post-2007 high, DB) break the falling-rate assumption under equity valuations therefore 37bp of hikes priced for year-end, 71% Oct (DB) therefore a 5yr auction tails 3.20bp on weak real-money demand (JPM), the mechanical reason the selloff extended. Activity-to-costs-to-policy: the fastest input-cost rise since 2020 (JPM) kills the disinflation case for a cut, so the Fed has to resume tightening and loses the ability to talk long yields down; Thursday's Fed speakers are confirmation, not news. JPM's counter-read: fair value is 5.5%, past overshoots have been buying opportunities, but JPM's own near-term equity stance stays cautious into the Fed meeting -- the auction tail is offered as the tell that 5.11% isn't yet cheap against that 5.5% anchor. Invalidation: the Sept 30 data (PCE) and whether yields close the gap to 5.5%.
why: The pulse reproduces both banks' argued steps in the same order and direction with correct attribution (DB for PMI/yield/hike-pricing, JPM for the auction tail, the input-cost detail, and the 5.5% fair-value/buy-the-dip view with its own cautious near-term stance), and its added framing ('the auction is the tell') combines two JPM data points rather than inventing a mechanism or reversing either bank's conclusion; only a minor unverified yield figure (5.16% vs. the sourced 5.141%) drifts, which doesn't alter the chain.
